utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one matter I could deal with while Mr. Delic is coming into court. Mr. Cepic, you've asked about exhibits from the bar table and the timing of any motion for these. It seems to us that these applications should be made at the earliest possible date now. If they're left until the end of your case, then it is going to be very difficult to deal with them in a reasonable way the closer we get to the end of the whole trial. It's in everyone's interests that everything is in our hands at the earliest possible opportunity. So albeit, there will be some that you will inevitably have to deal with at the close of your case. What we would like you to do is deal with the bulk of them as you go along even if it means making more than one application, so that those you are able to deal with now should be dealt with now and so on and another batch possibly when we come back after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, the same applies in your case, inevitably there will be documents you seek to have admitted. There's an even greater onus on you because of the position you have at the tail end of this to get your application in at a fairly early stage in the presentation of your case. We hope not to make an order about this; but unless we see some action in response, we will make an order and it's in everyone's interest to try to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have for our part submitted those documents already for translation so we hope to have translations, hopefully, by the time we get back from the winter recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that you've inquired about it and it is important I think that you understand what would be easiest in everyone's interests for the Trial Chamber to deal with. Good morning, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination by Mr. Cepic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the outset of your evidence will continue to apply to that evidence start to finish, and in particular applies to your evidence today. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We broke off with the beginning of the war. You made some markings on a map last night towards the end of our sitting hours. Could you tell me what the main tasks of your unit were from the beginning of the war onwards.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that my unit defended the state border directly, the basic task was the blocking defence of the border; the second was the protection of units and military facilities; the third task was the protection of roads and the territory, communication routes and the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you about to depart from this map now or are you going to continue with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Not now, Your Honour, maybe later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have any more information on the origin of this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map, 5D1332, appears to be the same map that was used in the Milosevic trial. It was Exhibit D300, tab 487. Now, Your Honour raised some questions about it at the time at transcript page 41908. Mr. Delic informed you at that time, Your Honour, that this was a photocopy of the map that he had used in 1999. You asked him where the original was and he said that was in Belgrade in the archive. So what this is appears to be a photocopy that was produced by Mr. Milosevic during this witness's testimony in July -- actually, July 6th, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, in war conditions, how did the command system function?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command system functioned in the usual way, nevertheless, it was hindered because the communications systems were destroyed. The first targets of the NATO aggressor during the first few days of the war, in addition to the PVO centres, were the communication centres of the Army of Yugoslavia. All centres of communications in Kosovo and Metohija were hit during the first few days, inter alia my communication centre was hit as well, and then civilian centres and repeaters were hit. So communications with our superior command were therefore impeded, and that's the way things were throughout the war. However, I can say that the communication system, both along horizontal and vertical lines, functioned as envisaged by the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, within your unit, did you have any volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within my unit there were several volunteers. They came from the centres where communications -- volunteers gathered in Belgrade and in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did they undergo a certain triage at these centres?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the centres their psychological and physical fitness were checked, how trained they were from the point of view of their military evidentiary specialty, and those who were fit from the point of view of their health were sent further on to Nis. And from Nis depending on the needs of the units involved and depending on the decisions made by the command, they were sent to our units. That is how I got them in my brigade too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you carry out additional triage within your brigade once they came in?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to establishment, a brigade has one psychologist in peacetime. In peacetime, I did not have a psychologist, but during the war I got two of them; one of them got killed during the war. And they were used precisely for that purpose, to tour units so that commanders and commanding officers could send soldiers, not only volunteers, but soldiers, reservists, to them because not everyone experiences war in the same way. Therefore, in accordance with the instructions of the psychologists, we sent some people further on, to military medical commissions, most often to Nis. And a number of people, I think that the percentage would be 1 per cent, perhaps a bit more than that, were released during the war. We released them because they were not capable, from the point of view of their health and psychologically speaking, to take part in combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit Number P02082, please. Thank you. I will follow your instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document, however, could it please be zoomed in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, is this your signature down there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document that was created on the basis of the order of the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We can see paragraph 1 here, paragraph 2 of this order. Does this confirm what you said to us previously?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order to my commanders and commanding officers to analyse all volunteers and reservists because for soldiers we already had all this information. I'm telling them to follow their behaviour and also that if they noticed that some of them seem distressed or disturbed in any way, they should be sent further on for medical check-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, in this courtroom the term "excessive use of force" has been used and continues to be used. Can you tell me whether your units engaged in excessive use of force?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my units specifically, I can say that it never used excessive force, not in 1998, not in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've already heard from General Maisonneuve about 1998, or rather, about your unit. Could you tell us how were combat resources used during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of the war, combat resources on the border during the operation Strela 2, Arrow 2, when the aggressor and enemy used everything known to the modern world, we used all the resources we had available. However, in this anti-terrorist struggle from the beginning of 1998 until the beginning of the aggression, combat resources were used on a selective basis. As for armoured equipment, tanks, they were there, but due to a large number of aggressor aircraft in the air, they practically did not open fire. Other equipment was used, weapons carried by soldiers or some that are manned by a few soldiers like recoilless guns, and so on, however, selectively in terms of firing points that were observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, I would be interested in the following. During the war period, did the institutions of the state function?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about my own zone here in particular. In my zone all institutions of the state did function in the town of Pristina, which is the head of the district; the district functioned; the municipality functioned; the judiciary; the prosecutor's office; the customs office; the taxation system; the health system absolutely; the public utilities. After all, this was also established by different journalists who came to the town of Prizren. All institutions of the system of the functioned up until the very last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, were units of the civil defence and civil protection resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the civil defence and civil protection were not resubordinated to me because they are linked to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all fairness, I saw the commander of civil defence a few times because he also had his obligations in terms of protecting facilities in the town of Pristina and he had the obligation to protect a few bridges. So in order to avoid any misunderstandings or any accidents, friendly fire and the like, before he took up the facilities that he was protecting he notified me that his unit is protecting those two bridges. According to the plan of use of units of civilian defence, that's the way it was supposed to be. Civilian protection units were engaged a few times when some parts of the town of Prizren were hit during the NATO bombing. They were dealing with the consequences there, providing relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Were MUP units resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MUP units were not resubordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia and in my zone to my unit. They had their own line of command, their own chain of command, and with them with regard to certain matters, when certain tasks were being carried out we had coordination with them, but otherwise we cooperated as state organs that are in a particular territory and that have certain obligations vis-a-vis each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just very briefly, did you have any losses due to terrorist activity and NATO attacks?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My unit had rather significant losses, especially in 1999. In 1998, due to terrorist attacks, I had four dead soldiers and four dead officers and 12 wounded soldiers. In 1999 in my unit or those that were linked to my unit, all in all, including 1998, there were 87 soldiers killed or in my zone, 96 soldiers killed and almost 300 wounded soldiers and -- now, was it 21 or 22 kidnapped soldiers. And we know today that they had all been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, Colonel Crosland testified before this Trial Chamber and he mentioned he knew you. On that occasion we discussed the issue of losses during the pull-out from Kosovo and Metohija. Did you have losses then as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met with Colonel Crosland just before the pull-out, and he was one of the leading men who visited my zone in 1998 and 1999 as part of the OSCE mission. He appeared again before the end of the war, but as an officer of the British army. I had six troops kidnapped and two dead during the pull-out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, it wasn't recorded. I have to repeat my question. What happened to those who were kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning one number of the kidnapped, two who were from Prizren, I know that they're dead because their bodies were handed over and buried, I believe, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you mentioned the Strela 2 action. Can you tell us what that was about, when it began, and which forces were involved, and whether there were any attacks on your unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strela 2 or Arrow 2 is an action organized jointly by terrorist forces and NATO forces. The terrorist forces attacked on land with the support of the artillery of the Albanian army, which was actively involved in the attack, and the aviation of the NATO alliance. This operation began early in the morning on the 26th of May and it lasted – it continued after those first negotiations- when the negotiations were--. The negotiations were already concluded, but NATO continued its air-strikes all the way up to 8th or 9th of June, after the signing. I also had losses in those last days of the war when it was already decided that the army would withdraw from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. NATO commander Wesley Clark says in his book: Although we signed the agreement, we continued to bomb them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That has been accurately translated, has it? Although we signed the agreement, we continued the air-strikes. Is that correct, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Correct. We can ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Delic, is that what you said: Although the agreement was signed, we continued the air-strikes, quoting Clark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement was signed already on the 3rd of June -- in fact, it was agreed, it was reached on the 3rd of June, and my last significant losses were on the 8th of June, that means four or five days after it was agreed in Belgrade that the war would stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a simple matter of precision. You said a moment ago that the strikes continued even after agreement had been reached, right up to the signing of the agreement. Then you are recorded as saying that even after the signing of the agreement, the bombing continued, according to Wesley Clark. Now, is that last part what you are actually saying, that the bombing was said to have continued after the agreement was actually signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard now several words in the interpretation that are simply not correct. It's somehow differently worded about those air-strikes. On the 3rd, as far as I remember, the 3rd of June, a cease-fire was agreed. My last losses and the last heavy bombardment by strategic aviation was on the 8th of June, and later I read in the book written by Wesley Clark these words: Although we agreed a cease-fire, we bombed them because we were thinking that Milosevic might renege on the agreement again. I can find later the exact page on Wesley Clark's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful, but please understand that what was translated for us was that after the signing of the agreement the bombing continued, according to Wesley Clark, and precision on this is important and the matter has now been clarified. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have on our screens Exhibit Number 5D916, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have just a partial translation of this document, but I spoke to my learned friend Mr. Hannis and I think that he hasn't got any objection about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I said that given the fact that it appears I won't have to start my cross-examination until next Tuesday, I think I will have an opportunity to see if I need a further translation. Mr. Cepic indicated he would request a full translation. In the meantime, I'll have time to consult with a language assistant, so I'm willing to proceed with this one today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an interim report from my brigade for the 27th of May, and it's obvious that I dictated it directly to the typist. And it recounts the beginning of the land attack in the Strela action on the axis Planeja. I explain that there are three combat lines and that if my officers noticed there were around 1.000 members of Siptar terrorist forces, massive artillery is being used, multiple rocket-launchers and mortars from the Albanian side by the Albanian army. By 1600 hours on the 27th, they managed to reach and capture a certain line into our territory. It also relates to our losses, our dead and wounded. And my main problem is I'm reporting to the commander is that we have a small number of soldiers and a very large area, so the defence does not have the necessary depth. The losses are one dead, four seriously wounded, and six less seriously wounded. I suggest certain measures to the commander, and I request that some of the corps artillery be sent to me to support my forces on this axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, which mountain is this where the combat took place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mount Pastrik. Its highest peak is 1980 [as interpreted] metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber let me say that the line of the border crosses the peak of that mountain, goes along the peak, and the peak of that mountain is on the elevation, it goes along the watershed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, what is the highest peak of that mountain?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1988 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again mistake in transcript, he said 1.000 -- oh, okay, that's fine. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you mentioned General Clark in his book. I would like exhibit P82 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. If we're going to introduce General Clark's book, let's introduce the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need one short paragraph for identification, not the whole book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the way for you to deal with this is to have any necessary passage read from the book. Mr. Hannis, you're going to have to justify introducing any passages at appropriate stages in cross-examination or wherever along the line you see the opportunity, and we'll address that as and when it arises. So please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have 5 -- P823, please, in B/C/S that is a page 185, in English it is the page 188, please. Right-hand page in English, also in B/C/S. Could you zoom in, please, page 371 in B/C/S. Thank you, that's perfect. In English, that is the page 335 -- the last paragraph, actually, paragraph before the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, would you please read the paragraph beginning with the words "on Monday morning ..."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, could my learned friend advise me where on the notification this exhibit was listed. I'm not finding it at the moment. Perhaps there was a supplementary, but I don't see it in my list of exhibits for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We informed -- we informed promptly -- we informed promptly OTP about this exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My assistant has been dealing with that issue and we will solve that as soon as is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it can hardly be said there's any prejudice to the Prosecution, who a moment ago wanted the whole book in, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, would you please read this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On Monday morning, we started receiving reports that the KLA was barely hanging onto the top of Mount Pastrik. At the video-televised conference, I could not have been clearer with Mike Short and Jay Hendrix. 'By 1.00,' I directed, 'you're going to tell me what you're going to do to help the KLA hold the top of that mountain. That mountain is not going to be lost. We're not going to have Serbs on the top of that mountain. We'll have to pay for the top of that hill with American blood if we don't help the KLA hold it now. That's my number-one priority.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, Your Honour, I just start it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do these words of General Clark confirm your assertion that the American army was helping the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was not aware of these words of Mr. Clark, but I felt in the field the full power of the NATO Alliance, which it was using against small tactical units such as those that I had on Mount Pastrik. On that day and the days that followed, in addition to bombing by regular aviation, aircraft F-16, A-10, and other aircraft that the Alliance had at its disposal, I experienced for the first time bombardment by strategic aviation, B-52 planes. On the ground it felt like being bombed by atomic bombs because the whole mountain was obscured by smoke and the mushrooms resulting from the B-52 bombing. This was carpet bombing, that is what it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was that bombing to provide support or was its significance different?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was direct support to the KLA. Strategic bombing was supposed to clear the way for the destruction of our units which were defending the state border to clear up the situation so that the KLA could break out as soon as possible into the Drina valley and arrive at the city of Prizren itself, just as the NATO spokesperson, Jimmy Shea had already announced one day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Jamie Shea, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, as a result of that bombing, were there any consequences in the villages on the border?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the villages were razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you enumerate some of these villages?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Planeja, Saj Mahala, Binaj, Ninaj, these are the ones I remember without looking at a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to us, Mr. Cepic, that nothing that has been said by Mr. Delic in relation to this matter depends on what's in the book, and you were very keen, as were a number of the other accused, to ensure that General Clark did not give evidence here and we refused to allow him to give evidence. It therefore seems, on the face of it, rather inappropriate that you should then start introducing his material without anyone having an opportunity to challenge him on it or hear what he has to say on it. Now, the situation may be different in another context and you may come to something else in the book that we have to address in particular, but for the moment it seems to us that none of the answers given by Mr. Delic are actually enhanced or depend in any way on what's in the book. It would be far better for us to hear continuously throughout this about his personal knowledge of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Delic, how many of your men were lost at Pastrik on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 29 soldiers were killed by NATO bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. General --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And about 200 soldiers were wounded. I'm saying that because the number of wounded is something I'm telling you, relying only on my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, were there any refugees just before the onset of the aggression?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the aggression began on the 24th, in the evening, and there was some refugees, although not very many, on the 24th. The population that was outside their houses had existed even before that period, but these were internally displaced persons. They remained on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The first refugees started on my territory on the 24th, and they turned up to a greater or lesser extent throughout the aggression; after the 15th or the 20th of April, this decreased in intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I continue, please? Thank you. Could we have on our screens Exhibit Number 5D885.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I myself wrote, addressing it to the corps commander and the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that here you mention a large number of refugees and that this is a major problem. Can you please explain the second paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second paragraph? "At our insistence a small number of persons returned to their places of residence, while others waited to be allowed to enter the Republic of Albania."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you mention the reasons they gave you when you interviewed them as to why they wanted to leave the country?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I enumerated the reasons here which I personally heard from the refugees in my interviews with them on the roads in the vicinity of Prizren and on the roads leading to the border. One of the reasons was fear of the impending fighting between our forces and the KLA and NATO on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what would be another reason?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of Siptars said they were leaving the country in order not to be forcibly mobilised into the KLA. A number of persons stated that they were afraid of the army and the police, especially Arkan's soldiers. I asked them if they had ever seen Arkan's army and not a single one of them could confirm that. They all said they had heard about it from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about (d), paragraph (d)?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it. Can the document be moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please. And page 2 in English and zoom out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fear of NATO bombing was emphasised as the primary reason because, as they said, they do not distinguish between troops and civilians and do not look where they are striking. My conclusion was that although in the first few days there had not been a lot of air-strikes on civilian targets. Most of them had been on military targets. We felt that this fear was realistic, although perhaps not to the extent expressed by the Siptars I spoke to. And then I further concluded that the refugees - and I found this interesting - had sufficient amounts of food with them, especially flour and oil. The corps commander wanted to know, because I was duty-bound to check whether the refugees had enough food, and I was supposed to list their needs. However, as there was a large number of these refugees and they were leaving the territory of our country, I only established and reported that they had sufficient amounts of food with them and that only on some occasions did we provide medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm interested in now. Who provided medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We provided medical assistance in Prizren because in Prizren, that's where my field hospital was located, and these were usually elderly people. Later on, in several instances when columns were bombed and some parts of town were bombed, in my field hospital or war hospital in Prizren which had four surgical teams and four operating theatres, we took care of most of the persons who were wounded when the columns were bombed. One column was bombed on the Djakovica-Prizren road and another on the Prizren-Suva Reka road, near the village of Korisa. And also when different parts of the town were bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we show page 2 in B/C/S and probably to scroll down in English. Could we a little bit scroll up in B/C/S, please. Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we see here that there were attempts to confiscate things from refugees, primarily money and vehicles. What did you do when you received such information?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that the road along which the refugees were moving passed through the combat disposition of my unit so that a certain number of soldiers tried to take money from those persons. And some also tried to take vehicles from them. They were all arrested. Criminal reports were filed and they were handed over to the security organs and then to the military court, the war court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In point 2, paragraphs 2 and 3, you say there was least movement in Gora and that 30 per cent of the population which was Serbian left the territory. Where did you get this information from, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I contacted the local self government bodies, and I knew that through my officers. All my officers had moved their families away, some to Macedonia, some to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and most to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did the units of your brigade apply the international laws of war and the Rules of Combat?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an imperative which was always pointed out whenever a task was issued to the commanders. According to the rules, in every order before executing combat activities, the commanders had to inform their subordinate units that the application of international humanitarian war and laws of war was obligatory, it was mandatory, and could not be departed from.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D888, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my document dated the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And pursuant to what did you issue this document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order coming from the Pristina Corps command dated the 16th of April, with a view to reducing casualties caused among the civilian population by aggressor fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned that refugees, or rather, the road leading to the border passed through the combat disposition of your unit. We have had Prosecution witnesses testifying here who said that on that road the troops stood on both sides of the road. Can you explain what this was about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. My soldiers, especially from the engineering battalion, stood on either side of the road, from the state border all the way to the village of Zur and in some places also in-depth. According to the plan for the use of my unit, it was envisaged that the entire territory from the very border itself and then along the depth should be laid with anti-armour and anti-infantry land-mines. The road itself, the Prizren-Vrbnica road, that is, had been prepared already in peacetime for demolition at the village of Zur. That was one point and the second was the bridge leading from the village of Zur towards Vrbnica and mine pits with 5 tonnes of explosives each were prepared there before the war, before the columns of refugees turned up. All that had already been completed before the refugees turned up. To avoid losses among the civilians, the soldiers had to stand along the sides of the road to prevent people from going off the asphalt road. It would have been enough for them to take one or two steps off the road and they might step on a land-mine. In a later period, we found tape which we stretched along either side of the road, but we still had to have men standing there, although a smaller number of men, to warn the civilians, to tell them that on that section of the road they must not take a single step off the road because they would activate land-mines and be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties due to that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two cases. One happened -- well, I did say at the very beginning that the road leading out of our country had been mined as well. When the refugees showed up, I had to demine that road; however, I demined only the right-hand lane of the asphalt road. On the left lane there were warnings. On one occasion, one of the drivers, one of the Albanians who was going to Albania, was not driving in a column, he went to the left lane, and he came across land-mines that were activated. And in that car there must have been several wounded and dead persons; however, since this is on the very border with Albania they were immediately transferred to Albanian territory. So I do not know about the destiny of these passengers and I don't know how many casualties there were actually. There was this other case when the police patrol was driving from Zur to Vrbnica in a Lada vehicle. They wanted to make a U-turn and come back to Prizren. Although they had been warned, they got off the asphalt road to the macadam road, a small byroad, only 1 and a half metres later they came across an anti-tank mine, their vehicle was destroyed, one person got killed, and the other person was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 5D891, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, is this your order and does it corroborate precisely the words you said just now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my order, and now I see that the incident with the police occurred on the 17th of April; after that, this order was written, prohibiting any movement off roads, Prizren-Vrbnica, and also along Djakovica-Cafa Prusit because this other road had also been completely mined. Again, this order requests that all unit members and the local population and refugees be warned of possible consequences and be told about this order, and that is why this order was submitted to the 2nd Motorised Battalion of my brigade that was in Prizren and to the MUP of Prizren and to the municipal assembly of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the transcript it says that it was submitted to the 2nd Battalion and to the municipality of Prizren and who else?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP in Prizren, the SUP of Prizren, Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P1988, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, is this a document of yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that was written by my operations officer and I signed it. He wrote it on my orders. This document is a response to the order of the Pristina Corps, strictly confidential 455-117 on the 23rd of April, and I am answering the same day. The document has to do with the following. I am informing the commander that all the military territorial detachments that are resubordinated to the 549th Motorised Brigade were relocated from populated areas and occupied sectors for defence pursuant to combat orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why were they relocated from populated areas and when were they relocated in your case?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the necessity was regarding this order because in my zone military territorial detachments were never in populated areas, in built-up areas. As soon as they were resubordinated to me, they immediately took up their own areas of defence of the state border. Only the command of the military department was in Prizren. However, perhaps in some other units, in-depth, there was a need to relocate them out of populated areas. If you look at my war map that you used a few moments ago, you will see that the deployment of these platoons in the -- on the state border in the municipality of Gora, in the municipality of Djakovica, and facing the Macedonian border, that is the 108th Detachment from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D897, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please have a look at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Should I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have it on our screens in front of us -- or actually, go ahead, read it out, but fast, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Receiving, dispersing, and providing security for the civilian population, act in line with the previously issued orders of the brigade command. Prevent any undisciplined behaviour on the part of commanding officers in relation to the civilian population (such as banning return to populated localities and so on)."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, we already heard testimony from a witness here that near Korisa members of the military were returning people to their villages and towns, K-79 was the Prosecution witness who said that. Could you tell us whether there were other such examples and whether these units near Korisa were from your unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the unit near Korisa could not have been from anybody else's unit but mine. That is a military territorial attachment. There were several cases. I personally returned civilians and talked to people who led some smallish columns. I asked them why they were going and I asked several times that they go back to their places of residence. However, there was a problem here. Through my border crossing people were leaving the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, because from my zone quite a few civilians went to the town of Prizren -- and even people from Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec were coming this way and from other towns and villages. It was a problem to have them returned. At one moment I even said that they could not cross the border, that the border was closed, and I said that they had to return to their respective towns and villages. Truth to tell, this column did go back, it was about 20 vehicles, and it went about 20 kilometres back to the area of the village of Rogovo. There is a greenhouse there where they sought shelter and stayed for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But later, later, they did leave. They didn't return to Mitrovica, they left, they crossed the border, too. As for one particular column that I stopped, I convinced them to go back; however, they told me then that they didn't have the fuel to do that, that they would go back if I can provide fuel for them. I could not provide that because I had fuel only for my own units, on a very restrictive basis. Then they said to me, The border with Albania is only 14 kilometres away. We have enough fuel to get to Albania, so let us go. In my zone we returned the population to a few villages, and later we went to these villages and guarded them because these villagers had told us that when they come back they might have problems with terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, we see paragraph 3 here, clearing up.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell me something about clearing up, clean-up. It says here that it is a priority task.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clean-up is a priority task and was in particular in my territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have special units -- special teams for that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had several teams. Clean-up means eliminating all danger in the territory threatening the civilian population and the military. In my territory there were a great many such threats. First of all, in some villages from which the civilian population had left, livestock stayed on and they wandered off into the fields. I don't know how well aware people are aware of this, but if cattle eat clover they die, so there was a lot of dead cattle strewn all over my territory. Also, there were many stray dogs attacking cattle. My territory was bombed with cluster bombs every day. These cluster bombs were all over the territory, so I had to have one team that went and buried the cattle. Another team went out to destroy cluster bombs. Yet another team went out to measure radioactivity where NATO had bombed. Yet another team went to have a look at parts of cluster bombs and other rocket projectiles with which my territory had been targeted, and that was all over the territory. They were trying to put them away so that the civilian population wouldn't have any contact with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit Number 5D1242, please. This is the video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have some technical problems. I hope that my assistant will solve that in a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is faster than expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I hope that we will solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this about an incident on which there is no dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I hope that we haven't got any dispute, but I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this damage --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is this damage caused by a NATO attack that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know which one this is supposed to be. I need some foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We still have technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's ask some questions then and see if the witness can help us. The film is meaningless until we get some context.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, this playback is rather fast. Do you recognise any of these scenes?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one does not belong to the rest. Where you see the road and the tractors that were hit, I recognise that. This is one NATO air-strike against the column of refugees on the 14th of April on the Prizren-Djakovica road that goes on to Meja and further on. I was there myself perhaps an hour or 90 minutes after the bomb hit them. The bombing took place in seven different locations along a stretch of 14 kilometres perhaps. This one that you see is the closest to Prizren. It's about 1 kilometre to the south-east from Pirane village, where one part of these -- this column, this convoy of refugees was hit. Another part of the convoy was hit right next to Pirane. One part of the convoy was hit next to Zrze; another part of the convoy was hit next to the bridge across the Drin river. Another part of the convoy was hit close to Bistrazin, close to the old bridge, and also close to Djakovica they were hit once. And they were hit close to Meja again. Out of those seven locations, I visited five going from Prizren to Djakovica. A large number of people were killed but NATO did not recognise it the first day. They admitted to it only two or three days later. I believe in Djakovica or the area that belongs to Djakovica, around 40 people were killed, a larger number was wounded. And in the section of the road close to Prizren, around 30 people were killed and a large number was wounded. In the war hospital in Djakovica, and especially in the war hospital in Prizren, we attended to those refugees who could still be helped. Their injuries were horrific. Limbs had to be amputated very frequently and there were horrible burns on their bodies. It was the 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, is there a report on this, a document that reports the facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 5D922.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not the best way --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is a combat report of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not the best way to deal with it? We know this exists --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- we can look at it another --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's just get on with the matters. There is no dispute about this. The witness acknowledges NATO admitted that this was their responsibility, so let's move on. We're not here to provide propaganda for countries in the Balkans. Let's get to the facts that really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting. Thank you one more time. Only problem, I'm afraid that we have partial translation but we will see. Could we have 5D922, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this a combat report of yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my combat report, but it relates to another air-strike, a different air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you explain about that different air-strike?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I reported the first, the second, and the third. This is the 21st of April, it says that at 3.00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's deal with this in order if you have to go through these documents with a witness in live time in court where there's no dispute, but if that's the way you want to use your time, then let's do it but let's do it in order. Let's have the report, first of all, for the one we've seen on the screen which was on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you don't want to use it, just give us the reference for it and we'll attend to it, but it's not 5D922.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I cannot find right now, this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you can give us the number of it later and now go to 5D922, which is on the screen, if that's the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- if that's the one you intend to deal with next.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, explain briefly this document before you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another one of my combat reports, but for the 21st April. It's just a few days after this first bombing. This one was the bombing of refugee settlement also in Bistrazin village a couple of kilometres from Djakovica, in the direction of Prizren. Refugees from the Republic of Serbian Krajina were put up there. The bombing took place at 3.00, four people were killed, and the 22 wounded were taken to the health centre in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D914, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we see that this one is a combat report from your brigade. What is written in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a combat report from my brigade for the 14th of May. In the first paragraph it says that during the night a refugee convoy was bombed in Korisa village. NATO aviation bombed this convoy that was travelling on convoys on way -- on the way home with more than 14 projectiles. It says that around a hundred, that is, a hundred, refugees were killed and many were wounded seriously or less seriously. Many of them are women and children, the wounded were taken to the health centre in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14th of May. It happened between midnight -- I believe the first bombs hit 20 minutes after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who did the bombing?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D910, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at paragraph 3: "On the 28th of April ..."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just tell us briefly what it is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 28th of April, 1999, around 2300 hours, a populated area between Ortokol and the suburb of Culjan in Prizren came under attack. The consequences were as follows: Four civilians were killed and seven were wounded. The civilians were Roma."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The date again?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report is dated 29th April and the incident happened on the 28th at 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How did you find out about this incident?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in Prizren itself, in the vicinity. Another part of my barracks is located, namely, the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How did you find out about the accident with the Korisa convoy on the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find about that immediately, although I could hear the explosions myself after midnight. But I heard the sound coming from the direction of Suva Reka where there were no units of mine. I learned about that only in the morning, the next morning, because the first wounded -- since the check-point of the MUP is perhaps 2 or 3 kilometres away from that location, the first wounded were brought to my hospital after 3.00 a.m., and I was notified around 4.00 a.m. because all the medical units - and I had four surgical teams - were engaged. We had to organize the giving of blood and to use the reserves of blood for transfusions to these refugees, the reserves that we were saving for our soldiers. I went to the site itself, but only later that day when the dead and wounded had been removed. I just inspected the site of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did members of your unit give blood for the victims?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous incident and on a number of times during the war, our troops gave blood, donated blood, but first we used the reserves of blood we had in our war hospital. So we first intervened with blood supplies that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back for a moment to the document on the screen, 5D910, the attack was against a feature, is it the Cvilen feature. What is that, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking about the incident I've just spoken about with the settlement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one on the 28th of April, the document relating to it is on the screen, paragraph 3 you were directed to and you'll see a reference to the feature that was being attacked by NATO; what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. First there is an account of this attack against the convoy of civilians and then other features are enumerated that were bombed. Cvilen feature is actually a hill holding a repeater for television broadcasts and for post communications. When this repeater was destroyed, all the communications between Kosovo and Metohija and the outside world were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The civilian communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the paragraph that's been translated. Was it in that attack that the civilians were killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That Cvilen feature, that is, the repeater station and TV repeaters are located on a hill overlooking Prizren. They were hit 30 times. The first time it was targeted there were people inside, but as far as I know nobody was killed. After that, this facility was abandoned, but it continued to be targeted until its aerial was destroyed. I believe it was completely finally destroyed in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how far is it from the populated area which is referred to later in the paragraph where the civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The populated area is several kilometres away, perhaps as the crow flies 10 kilometres or 15 kilometres by road. But that Cvilen hill is visible from Prizren, it is a dominant feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let us clear up one thing. This donation of blood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the witness has told us that first there is a reference to an attack against a convoy of civilians in this document, that must be a part that's not translated, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. We firstly spoke about incident in Korisa, and this is another document. This document is related just for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but in the first two paragraphs of this document is there any reference to an attack on civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the third one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Cepic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's just clarify, General, what we've just been saying about blood donations by members of your unit. What event was that connected to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had to do with the event when the convoy was bombed near Korisa. That was when the men gave blood, but one should know that today blood is not donated right away. It has to be processed first. We had several hundred men who were ready to donate blood at any moment always. We had blood in reserve, stocks of blood, which had already been prepared for operations, and we used those stocks, those reserves whenever we assisted civilians. And then people turned up on their own initiative offering to donate blood when they heard about this huge misfortune.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What men were you referring to? Were they your soldiers? Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily I'm referring to my soldiers, although I know that there were also civilians, citizens, who also turned up at the hospital to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We have seen three incidents so far in which civilians were killed. Let's now deal with a fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D1374, please. This is a short video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, what is this video about, the one we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the bombing of Prizren. I remember, it's Podrimska Street, and this bombing was by day, only one or two days after this bombing in an area inhabited by Albanians and Roma in that part of the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, we saw some young people in green camouflage uniforms in the video. Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you may have observed that some of them had the red cross sign on their left arm. Those were men from my medical corps. One of them was a squad leader at ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a convenient time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, would you leave the courtroom, please, and God willing, we'll continue at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: ---Recess taken at 10.47 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The force is toying with us, Mr. Cepic, but we shall proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Again the same problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've got a microphone and you've got a screen, so continue until there's a complete breakdown. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Lights, camera, action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My learned friend, Mr. Sepenuk, already told me that I'm almost like some editor, one famous Steven Spielberg, and I really appreciate that. Thank you and thank you to Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we saw that video clip and we saw members of your units assisting civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D911, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you look at point 4, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a combat report, a daily combat report, from my brigade for the 1st of May, and item 4 here -- yes. It's in item 4 that there is mention of what we have just seen, that the enemy aviation at 1200 hours hit three civilian buildings immediately next to the barracks with two projectiles. "According to current reports, two people were killed and two were seriously wounded." And then it goes on to say that: "The aviation also launched an attack on Jablanica village and the general area of Suva Reka. There are casualties but we do not have exact information at this time."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, does this combat report refer to the incident we saw on that video before the break?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a report that was subsequently sent to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw your soldiers, we listed four incidents, you explained that the soldiers were assisting civilians. Will you tell me, please, whether you had any special units in your brigade to look after civilians.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's an order which we've already seen here to the effect that every unit had to designate a certain group to provide assistance. But in situations such as this one, evidently, my medical company provided assistance because I recognised one of the company -- the company leader, but you could also see the civilian protection as well as ordinary citizens. And the firefighters also, everybody participated who was in the town of Prizren, all the institutions and ordinary citizens as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please describe something we saw on the clip. What uniforms do members of the civilian protection wear?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those blue uniforms you saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do they have fluorescent armbands?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are members of the civilian protection. That's how they were distinguished from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you explain the following three concepts: Zone of responsibility, area for defence, position for defence.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility or area of responsibility is the broadest of these terms. It designates a piece of territory and demarcation line between the different units in the Pristina Corps, and there is a war zone and a peacetime zone. The peacetime zone is considerably broader, and in the case of my unit it was over 4.000 square kilometres in size. The war zone is narrower, it's smaller, and it was a little less than 3.000 square kilometres. I had a very long length of border to secure. The defence area is a narrower term; it is a piece of territory taken by army units, fortified by the engineers, from which they defend themselves. Usually there is the basic area of defence, the reserve area of defence in depth, and then there is also the term the next area of defence. The positions are given to lower-level units at platoon level, and that is a small area taken up by the platoon where it builds its trenches and shelters. It's about 300 to 400 metres long if we're dealing with a platoon, and as each position has a reserve position in depth, it's also 300 to 400 metres in depth. When we are dealing with a company, its area of defence is a kilometre to a kilometre and a half along the front line, and the same amount of kilometres in depth. Battalions have 3 to 5 kilometres by some 3 kilometres. Between these units, there are areas in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You indicated on the map what your area of responsibility was. You explained the defence positions. I'm interested -- we've also heard about the length of that. Was there a lot of space in between the units?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this space in between the units is also envisaged in the rules. But especially in my situation when I was defending an area five times larger than envisaged by the rules, then the space in between also had to be much bigger. The rules provide that this in-between area should be protected, it should be observed, patrols should be sent in there, and sometimes mine are laid in these in-between areas, minefields are laid, regardless of whether they are anti-personnel or anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My understanding of that evidence is that we have a definition for an area of responsibility and a definition for an area of defence, and you asked about a third category which seemed to be position for defence. Is that something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is there a definition of that there?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Witness answered to us and I can ask him again just to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I see a zone of responsibility and then we had defence area is a narrower term, it's a basic area of defence, reserve area of defence in depth, and then there's also the term the next area of defence. The positions are given to lower-level units. Is that something different at that point or are we still dealing with, essentially, the area of defence? Can you clarify that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have an explanation now of the zone or area of responsibility. Could you please now explain the difference between the area of defence and the position for defence.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, areas of defence are assigned to larger units, for example, platoons, companies, and battalions. As I said, a platoon has its area of defence and sometimes it's called resistance points, and it's 300 to 400 metres by 300 to 400 metres in area, and a company and battalion have larger areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between area of defence and position for defence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can say that the position for defence is a line taken up by the basic unit. That is the place where shelters are erected, where the smallest units, squads, are located. There is the basic position and reserve position. The basic position is where there is fighting and the reserve position can be a certain distance behind that, about a hundred metres, 150 metres behind that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be useful if the witness draw us on the map just for clarification with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It wouldn't assist me, but it's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We've seen members of the police on the footage, we've seen members of the civilian protection. You've also mentioned the commander of the civil defence in Prizren, you did that in the previous part of your testimony. I would like to know whether you or any of your subordinates in the brigade had effective control. Did anyone have effective control over any of these units?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's absolutely clear. All my officers had effective control over our own units, as did I. We had no control over what -- whatsoever over MUP units or units of civilian protection or defence; they all had their own chains of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, K-54 was a Prosecution witness who testified before this Trial Chamber, K-89 as well, and K-89 [In English] K-82 and K-89, please. [Interpretation] And they said that in 1998, in basic training centres, they had training that was abbreviated. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are soldiers. Quite simply, they do not know what the teaching plan and programme is. It is correct that they spent the first stage of training in these training centres, which for them, like for all others, is two months and 20 days. The second stage of this basic training continues in the units. When a driver comes to my unit, he has to be trained additionally. He cannot drive straight away. We have to see what kind of vehicles he drove in the centre and what kind of vehicles he's going to drive in the unit. And then we have to see what the specific vehicles assigned to him are going to be, and then he is tested on those vehicles. And that practically goes on until the end of his term, because after the first stage comes the stage of the training of units, and that differs depending on the military evidentiary specialty of the soldier concerned. It varies in arms and services. As far as I can see, these two were in services and their training lasts that long precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleagues tell me that there's a mistake in the transcript, page 40, lines 23 and 24, it says K-54 trained as a soldier -- [In English] K-89 -- 82, actually, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have on my screen 42, page, and lines 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The spelling of the place?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It was not just the place. (redacted) (redacted) their speciality, and with your leave I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's clear. K-54 trained as a soldier, (redacted) Now, what's -- if you want to change that, you better ask Mr. Delic to explain it or, alternatively, you tell me what is wrong with that record of your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can be of assistance. The technical service trains in Senta, in Kraljevo. If training was in Kraljevo, then that is where drivers are trained; and this other soldier, if he came from Valjevo, Pirot, Podgorica, that is where infantrymen were trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, these witnesses, especially K-89 and K-54, say that they were not aware of provisions of international humanitarian law and rules pertaining to armed conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are compulsory subjects in basic training. Now I cannot talk about what was done in their centres because I was not there specifically when they were trained. However, there is a compulsory subject, familiarization with these provisions, and after all there is a compulsory teaching of the Rules of Service. And the Rules of Service actually refer to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did every soldier have instructions on the use of rules?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon arriving in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, because in 1998 only the territory of Kosovo and Metohija had been engulfed by terrorism, all soldiers received this instruction and all of them were duty-bound to have in the pockets of their shirts a copy of these instructions. It is brief. It explained the procedure of soldiers in different situations, and in the briefest possible terms the provisions of international humanitarian law on the treatment of civilians were expressed in detail there. The soldiers were issued with that and then they had to return these copies when leaving their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, Witness K-54 says that he was a soldier in your logistics battalion and that he had the duty of driver. And that in 1998 in the village of Damjane, he heard from a soldier that you had ordered his lieutenant-colonel to have the village cleansed of civilians with the following words: Get rid of all the civilians from this village. Is that assertion of his correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether such a statement merits any kind of comment whatsoever, because this is not military vocabulary, this is not an order that can be given by a professional officer. In the village of Damjane in 1998, there was a military unit but only in part of the village of Damjane. That part of the village of Damjane is called Mahadri Mahala. The village of Damjane is an enormous village in terms of the territory it covers, and there are several Mahalas that the army absolutely never entered in 1998, all the way up until the month of September or October. That was an artillery unit that, in front of Mahadri Mahala, had its artillery positions. That is about a kilometre and a half or two away from Rogovo in the direction of the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever issue, perhaps in a different situation, that kind of order to your subordinate officers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I personally. It is not only that I never issued such an order, but I'm certain that not a single one of my officers would have dared issue that kind of order because that would have meant a violation of all military rules, regulations, Rules of Service, laws. And since we're talking about 1998, it would be a violation of these humanitarian principles of international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.
